items.basis: The proposed mechanism fails to address the fundamental fragmentation issue as GPU virtual memory management (VMM) does not solve the physical memory allocation problem when dealing with mixed-length bursty requests, which the evidence ([doi:10.5220/0015138800004103]) shows causes KV cache fragmentation at the hardware level regardless of virtualization.

The candidate violates the boundary condition of "memory-bound LLM inference with KV cache fragmentation issues" as the vTensor approach introduces additional memory management overhead when switching between different model architectures, contradicting the known failure mode and making it unsuitable for multi-tenant environments.

The candidate's own evidence ([doi:10.1109/icassp55912.2026.11461518]) on MIDAS demonstrates that dynamic KV cache management across GPU systems introduces significant overhead, directly contradicting the claim that decoupling computation from memory defragmentation will reduce latency.

The predicted effect of reducing p99 first-token latency below 800ms at 3x baseline burst load is equivalent to the baseline under known failure modes, as the evidence ([doi:10.70675/036b4171z0acfz4a50z9d51z481b92e5f4da]) shows fundamental limits of shared-cache networks that cannot be overcome by virtual memory management alone.

The vTensor structure cannot be implemented as described because GPU virtual memory management systems are designed for page-level operations, not tensor-level management, as evidenced by ([doi:10.5463/thesis.308]) which highlights the latency-critical nature of inference serving making such abstraction prohibitively expensive.

The testable prediction fails to pin down the measurement methodology, as the evidence ([doi:10.14711/thesis-hdl152583]) on resource-efficient model serving demonstrates that performance metrics vary significantly based on multi-tenant configurations and request patterns, making the claimed 40% reduction unverifiable in real-world deployments.
